relationships.description: Connects RBAC Policy Design to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Grouping permissions into scoped, deny-by-default roles with Separation of Duties and OPA/Cedar policy-as-code.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of RBAC—from NIST Core/Hierarchical/SoD tiers to preventing role explosion, cross-tenant IDORs, and stale JWT permissions.

spark.summary: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) decouples permissions from individual users by grouping privileges into named roles, simplifying least-privilege governance and auditing at scale.
spark.keyTakeaway: Model roles around stable job functions—not ad-hoc org charts—enforce deny-by-default evaluation with Separation of Duties (SoD), and shift fine-grained resource-level checks to ABAC/ReBAC before RBAC explodes into thousands of bespoke roles.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** inserts a **Role** indirection layer between **Principals** ($U$) and **Permissions** ($P$: `action` + `resource_type`), reducing $U \times P$ direct ACL edges to $U \to R$ and $R \to P$.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts RBAC + Tenant-Scope Policy Decision State Machine (EVALUATE PDP -> ALLOW + AUDIT -> DENY (403)); Zero-Trust RBAC + Tenant-Scope Evaluation Flow (Envoy PEP -> OPA Sidecar PDP -> IdP / SCIM Sync -> Audit Log).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Select the simplest model that captures your granularity without role explosion. Envoy (Policy Enforcement Point) validates the OIDC JWT and calls a co-located OPA sidecar (Policy Decision Point) with `(sub, tenant_id, action, resource)`.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore OIDC authentication, OAuth2 flows, and zero-trust service boundaries.

learningJourney.title: What is RBAC Policy Design
learningJourney.explanation:
**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** inserts a **Role** indirection layer between **Principals** ($U$) and **Permissions** ($P$: `action` + `resource_type`), reducing $U \times P$ direct ACL edges to $U \to R$ and $R \to P$.

NIST RBAC defines four tiers: **Core** (User-Role-Permission), **Hierarchical** (`Admin > Editor > Viewer`), **Static Separation of Duties (SoD)** (mutually exclusive role assignment, e.g., cannot hold both `PaymentCreator` and `PaymentApprover`), and **Dynamic SoD** (mutually exclusive active session roles).

sectionDiagram.title: RBAC + Tenant-Scope Policy Decision State Machine
sectionDiagram.summary: Every authorization check must bind to an explicit tenant/resource scope and enforce explicit-deny-overrides-allow.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how RBAC Policy Design works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Structured RBAC (Role Explosion & Cross-Tenant IDOR)
learningJourney.explanation: Direct user-to-permission ACLs become un-auditable past a few dozen employees, leaving orphaned admin rights on offboarding. Conversely, poorly designed RBAC fails via **Role Explosion** (creating thousands of bespoke roles like `ProjectA_ReadOnly_NoExport_EU`) and **Cross-Tenant IDOR** (checking `hasRole('Editor')` without verifying `resource.tenant_id == user.tenant_id`).

ideas.title: Keep JWTs Thin; Resolve Permissions at the PDP
ideas.description: Stuffing 200 permissions into a JWT hits 4–8 KB HTTP header limits and delays role revocation until token expiry—store only `sub` and `session_id` in the JWT.

ideas.title: SCIM Lifecycle + Quarterly Recertification
ideas.description: Automate role grants/revocations via IdP/SCIM group sync to eliminate privilege creep when employees switch teams.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Structured RBAC under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where RBAC excels (and when to layer ABAC or ReBAC)
learningJourney.explanation: Use RBAC for functional personas and compliance SoD; layer ABAC (OPA/Cedar) for contextual attributes and ReBAC (Zanzibar) for document-graph sharing.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Enterprise SaaS & Cloud Control Planes
benefits: Clean functional roles (`Viewer`, `Editor`, `BillingAdmin`) + Namespace/Tenant bindings satisfy SOC 2 / ISO 27001 audits.
costs: Requires strict scope binding on every internal gRPC/GraphQL endpoint, not just the API gateway.

comparison.choice: Avoid Pure RBAC: Consumer Folder/Doc Sharing
benefits: Use ReBAC (Google Zanzibar / SpiceDB) when permissions inherit across arbitrary folder/team graphs.
costs: Modeling per-document roles in pure RBAC causes catastrophic role explosion.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Policy-as-Code (OPA/Rego) & Negative CI Tests are managed
learningJourney.explanation: Decouple policy decisions into a Policy Decision Point (**OPA** or **AWS Cedar**) stored in Git, log both `ALLOW` and `DENY` with `policy_version`, and block PR merges unless negative tests (cross-tenant isolation, SoD conflicts, explicit deny) pass.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```rego
# OPA Rego policy: Deny-by-default RBAC + Tenant Scope + Separation of Duties
package authz

default allow := false

allow if {
  not deny
  input.subject.tenant_id == input.resource.tenant_id
  some role in input.subject.roles
  input.action in data.role_permissions[role]
}

deny if {
  # Separation of Duties: creator cannot approve their own wire transfer
  input.action == "payment:approve"
  input.resource.created_by == input.subject.id
}
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Pure RBAC vs. RBAC + ABAC Hybrid vs. ReBAC
learningJourney.explanation: Select the simplest model that captures your granularity without role explosion.

benefits: Keeps 5–10 clean roles while expressing `env == prod` or `region == eu` via attributes.
costs: Requires passing clean resource/environment attributes to the PDP.

benefits: Models recursive folder/org ownership graphs naturally.
costs: Higher infrastructure complexity (graph traversal + consistency zookies).

comparison.choice: Stateless JWT Role Claims vs. Stateful PDP
benefits: Zero network hop if roles are embedded in short-lived (5m) tokens.
costs: Revocation lags until expiry and large permission lists bloat HTTP headers.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Envoy PEP + Sidecar OPA PDP + Audit Stream
learningJourney.explanation: Envoy (Policy Enforcement Point) validates the OIDC JWT and calls a co-located OPA sidecar (Policy Decision Point) with `(sub, tenant_id, action, resource)`. OPA evaluates the scoped Rego bundle in <1 ms, emits an immutable audit event, and pushes cache invalidations on SCIM role revocations.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is embedding 150 fine-grained permission strings directly inside a 60-minute OIDC/OAuth JWT an anti-pattern?

options.text: It bloats HTTP headers past 4–8 KB limits and prevents immediate revocation when a user is demoted or offboarded
options.feedback: Correct: keep JWTs thin (identity/session ID) and resolve permissions at a PDP with fast revocation.

options.text: Because JWTs cannot encode JSON arrays
options.feedback: JWTs can encode arrays, but header size limits and revocation lag make large permission claims problematic.

options.text: Because OPA cannot parse JWT signatures
options.feedback: OPA has built-in JWT verification; the issue is header bloat and stale permissions.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
